canonicalExplanation.summary: C++ projects split code into **headers** (`.h`/`.hpp`) and **source files** (`.cpp`). The header holds **declarations**: class definitions (members and method prototypes), free-function prototypes, and anything that must be visible everywhere it's used, meaning **templates**, `inline` functions and `constexpr` values. The source file holds the **ordinary definitions**: function bodies and member functions defined outside the class, each compiled **once**. **Include guards** (`#pragma once`) only stop a header being pasted twice into **one** .cpp; they do **nothing** about the same function being defined in **several** .cpp files. That's a link error the ODR forbids.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner moves `double average(const std::vector<int>& v) { ... }` into gradebook.h "to keep things together", reasoning that `#pragma once` will prevent duplicates. Two .cpp files include it and linking fails with multiple definition of average. A class declaration and function prototype live in a guarded header while one .cpp file defines non-inline member functions. In this lesson you'll create a multi-file function library with correct declarations and definitions.

```predict
{"question": "Does #pragma once stop a function defined in a header from being defined twice across two .cpp files?", "options": ["Yes", "No: it only prevents double inclusion within a single .cpp"], "answer": 1, "why": "Each .cpp is compiled separately, so each gets its own copy."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Loops and range iteration**, **Calls, parameters and returns**, **Function contracts and return values** and **Compile and link model** (ODR and templates in headers).

sections.heading: The rule: declare in headers, define ordinary functions once
Self-contained headers

includes: Put class definitions, prototypes, templates and inline functions in guarded headers.
Define ordinary and out-of-class member functions once in a .cpp, and keep headers self-contained.

outcomes: Create a multi-file function library with correct declarations and definitions.

examples.title: Gradebook split into .h and .cpp
examples.situation: A class declaration and function prototype live in a guarded header while one .cpp file defines non-inline member functions.
walkthrough: **A class declaration and function prototype live in a guarded header:** Gradebook and letter() in gradebook.h with #pragma once.
**One .cpp file defines non-inline member functions:** add, average and letter are defined only in gradebook.cpp.
**Build:** main.cpp and report.cpp both include the header; g++ main.cpp report.cpp gradebook.cpp will link cleanly.
examples.result: Any number of files can use the library without duplicate definitions.

examples.title: The helper that had to be inline
examples.situation: A tiny `int clamp_score(int s)` is defined in a header for speed and breaks the link.
walkthrough: Mark it inline so identical definitions are allowed,
or keep only its declaration in the header and define it in the .cpp.
Modern compilers inline across files anyway with optimisation.
examples.result: The helper works from every file, and the program links.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Moving any function definition into a header is safe because include guards prevent duplicate definitions at link time.
misconceptions.correction: Include guards act within one translation unit. Every .cpp including the header compiles its own definition, so non-inline definitions in headers violate the ODR.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why didn't #pragma once help?

analogy.example: A header is like **a restaurant menu handed to every table**: it lists dishes (declarations) so everyone can order. The kitchen (one .cpp) cooks each dish. Printing the full recipe on every menu and having every table cook it (definitions in headers) means the bill (linker) sees the same dish made many times.
limitations: Some dishes are served pre-made at every table: inline and templates.
The include guard stops a table getting two menus, not two kitchens.

steps.explanation: A class declaration and function prototype live in a guarded header.

nearTransfer.prompt: Split a single-file program with a class and two free functions into a header, a .cpp and main.cpp. Prove the header is self-contained with a .cpp that includes only it.
scaffold: Include the header in its own .cpp.

farTransfer.prompt: Build a small library (header + .cpp) used from two other .cpp files, containing a class, a free function, an inline helper and a function template. Reproduce the multiple-definition error by removing inline, then fix it and explain the ODR rule.

remediation.explanation: For each definition ask: **is it a template, inline or constexpr?** Then it may live in the header. **Otherwise**, only its declaration goes there; its body goes in exactly one .cpp.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The helper that had to be inline".

recap.summary: To build a multi-file library correctly, put class definitions, prototypes, templates, inline and constexpr items in self-contained guarded headers, define ordinary functions and out-of-class members once in a matching .cpp, and remember include guards don't prevent duplicate definitions across translation units.
retrievalPrompts: Where do ordinary function bodies go?
Why can member functions defined in the class live in headers?
